                     composition, and neuromuscular coordination, which are crucial for strength and power
                     development [1,2].
                           High-load resistance training (e.g., 80% 1 RM) induces superior neural adaptations
                     compared to low-load training (e.g., 30% 1 RM), as evidenced by increased voluntary acti-
                     vation and electromyographic (EMG) amplitude during maximal force production. These
                     findings suggest that high-load training more effectively improves the nervous system’s
                     ability to recruit and activate motor units, leading to more significant strength gains despite
                     similar muscle hypertrophy levels between high- and low-load training [1,2]. Additionally,
                     electrostimulation resistance training can shift muscle fiber composition towards Type I
                     fibers, benefiting endurance performance [3]. Neuromuscular adaptations also enhance
                     coordination and efficiency in muscle recruitment patterns, which is particularly significant
                     for repetitive and explosive movements in sports like running and cycling. Highly trained
                     athletes exhibit more refined muscle recruitment patterns than novices, contributing to
                     improved movement efficiency and performance output [4,5].
                           These adaptations are vital for sports requiring rapid acceleration, maximal force out-
                     put, and sustained high-intensity efforts, such as rugby, football, basketball, weightlifting,
                     and sprinting, where strength and power are key performance factors. Strength is essential
                     for lifting, pushing, tackling, and jumping, while power is critical for sprinting, striking,
                     and explosive directional changes. High levels of both attributes directly enhance sprint
                     speed, vertical jump height, and tackling efficiency [6–8]. Moreover, improved neuromus-
                     cular control and muscle stability contribute to injury prevention by reducing the risk of
                     musculoskeletal injuries [7–9]. By adopting training methods that optimize neuromuscular
                     adaptations, athletes can significantly enhance strength, power, and overall performance,
                     making these adaptations a fundamental aspect of sports science and high-performance
                     training [9–11].

                     1.2. Overview of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT)
                          High-intensity interval Training (HIIT) is a structured exercise method involving
                     short bursts of high-intensity effort (typically 20 s to a few minutes at 80–95% of maxi-
                     mal heart rate), alternated with low-intensity recovery periods [12]. This review focuses
                     specifically on HIIT and its primary protocol variations—sprint-based, resistance-based,
                     and plyometric-integrated formats—while other training methods are only discussed for
                     comparative context. Designed to maximize cardiovascular, metabolic, and neuromuscu-
                     lar adaptations more efficiently than traditional endurance training, HIIT enhances both
                     anaerobic and aerobic energy systems, leading to improved muscle strength, power, and
                     endurance [13–16]. Key principles of HIIT include intensity management and work-to-rest
                     ratios, where high-intensity phases demand near-maximal effort, and recovery intervals
                     are adjusted based on specific training goals. HIIT is highly adaptable, incorporating
                     sprinting, cycling, bodyweight drills, resistance exercises, and plyometrics to suit various
                     athletic needs [12]. Neuromuscular adaptations from HIIT involve enhanced motor unit
                     recruitment, Type II muscle fiber transformations, and improved energy system efficiency,
                     contributing to greater strength, power, and endurance [17–19].
                          Unlike traditional strength training, which focuses on progressive overload and maxi-
                     mal force output with more extended rest periods, HIIT simultaneously integrates high-
                     intensity dynamic movements that challenge the cardiovascular and neuromuscular sys-
                     tems [20]. While strength training develops maximal force production, HIIT emphasizes
                     shorter recovery to maintain elevated heart rates and metabolic demands, enhancing
                     neuromuscular efficiency, power endurance, and energy utilization [21]. Compared to
                     traditional endurance training, which primarily targets the aerobic system through pro-
                     longed, moderate-intensity efforts (60–70% HRmax), HIIT engages both anaerobic and

                     aerobic pathways, resulting in faster cardiovascular adaptations, improved muscle oxygen
                     utilization, and higher power output. Studies indicate that HIIT can match or surpass
                     traditional endurance training in enhancing endurance, strength, and power within a
                     shorter timeframe [16,21,22].
                           Integrating HIIT with conventional strength and endurance training helps athletes
                     build a well-rounded physical profile, optimizing strength, power, agility, and metabolic
                     efficiency. This approach enhances sports performance and aids in injury prevention by
                     improving muscle stability and neuromuscular control, making HIIT a valuable component
                     of high-performance training programs [22].

                     1.3. Purpose of the Review
                          This review examines the role of HIIT in neuromuscular adaptations, focusing on
                     motor unit recruitment, muscle fiber composition, and neuromuscular efficiency in strength
                     and power development. HIIT enhances motor unit activation, Type II fiber recruitment,
                     and neuromuscular coordination, all of which contribute to more excellent force production,
                     explosive power, and movement efficiency. Its applications extend beyond athletic perfor-
                     mance to rehabilitation, aiding muscle activation, movement control, and injury recovery.
                     However, despite the growing body of literature on HIIT and neuromuscular adaptations,
                     few reviews systematically address the gaps in the literature regarding the use of HIIT in
                     specialized populations such as youth athletes and patients undergoing rehabilitation. This
                     review aims not only to synthesize current knowledge but also to highlight underexplored
                     areas for future research.

                     2. Literature Selection and Scope
                           This review adopts a narrative approach to synthesize recent evidence on the neu-
                     romuscular adaptations induced by High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT), specifically
                     focusing on strength and power development. The objective is to provide an integrative
                     overview of current findings, highlight key mechanisms, and discuss practical applications
                     for athletes and practitioners.
                           Relevant literature was identified through a targeted search of peer-reviewed journal
                     articles published between 2000 and 2025, using databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web
                     of Science, and EBSCO. Search terms included combinations of the following keywords:
                     “high-intensity interval training”, “HIIT”, “neuromuscular adaptations”, “motor unit
                     recruitment”, “strength development”, “power output”, and “athletic performance”.
                           Articles were selected based on their relevance to the review’s core themes: (1) the
                     physiological and neuromuscular responses to HIIT; (2) strength and power outcomes in
                     athletic populations; and (3) training methods involving sprint-based, resistance-based,
                     and plyometric-based HIIT protocols.
                           Both original research articles and review papers were considered to ensure a broad
                     representation of current knowledge. Studies involving both trained and untrained ath-
                     letes were included. The selection emphasized findings applicable to sports performance
                     enhancement, rather than clinical rehabilitation or general fitness.
                           Rather than following a systematic inclusion/exclusion framework, this review em-
                     phasizes conceptual integration and thematic synthesis, drawing connections between
                     neuromuscular principles and HIIT methodologies. Key themes were organized into
                     sections on motor unit recruitment, muscle fiber adaptations, neuromuscular efficiency,
                     strength and power development, and training strategies.
                           This approach allows for a more flexible and comprehensive discussion of emerging
                     trends, gaps in the literature, and practical implications for strength and conditioning.

                     3. Mechanisms of Neuromuscular Adaptations to HIIT
                           High-intensity interval training promotes neuromuscular adaptations that enhance
                     motor unit recruitment, muscle fiber composition, neuromuscular efficiency, and metabolic
                     function, improving strength, power, and endurance. These adaptations, driven by neu-
                     ral, muscular, and metabolic mechanisms, collectively boost force production, movement
                     efficiency, and fatigue resistance, offering valuable insights into how HIIT optimizes per-
                     formance for athletes across various sports. Unless otherwise specified, the following
                     mechanisms are synthesized from the 86 studies included in our systematic search.

                     3.1. Motor Unit Recruitment and Neural Drive
                           Effective at inducing neuromuscular adaptations, HIIT enhances motor unit recruit-
                     ment, synchronization, and firing frequency. Research demonstrates that HIIT significantly
                     increases the activation of fast-twitch fibers, which are essential for explosive movements
                     such as sprinting and jumping. The intense demands of HIIT improve recruitment efficiency
                     by engaging a more significant number of motor units [23,24]. Additionally, HIIT promotes
                     better synchronization of motor units, leading to more coordinated muscle contractions,
                     which is critical for rapid and robust movements [25]. By repeatedly targeting a broad
                     pool of fast-twitch fibers, HIIT enhances explosive power enabling muscles to generate
                     force quickly—an essential factor for short-burst activities that rely on RFD [24,26]. The
                     impact on neural drive is another significant benefit, as HIIT improves signal transmission

HIIT an effective strategy for improving endurance and overall performance.
                           In addition to the acute and mid-term neuromuscular adaptations discussed earlier,
                     several studies have examined the long-term effects of HIIT on sustained improvements in
                     strength and power. These long-term adaptations appear to be influenced by individual
                     characteristics, including genetic predispositions, muscle fiber composition, and recovery
                     capacity, highlighting the importance of personalized programming approaches [32]. More-
                     over, when adequately periodized, the integration of HIIT with traditional strength and
                     plyometric training has been shown to enhance both power output and endurance capacity
                     without causing interference effects. This supports the role of HIIT as a valuable com-
                     plementary component within comprehensive performance training frameworks [26]. In
                     rehabilitation contexts, HIIT has also demonstrated the potential to restore neuromuscular
                     function following injury or periods of immobilization. Evidence suggests that structured
                     HIIT protocols can enhance motor unit recruitment, proprioceptive control, and muscle
                     reactivation, making it a practical option for early-phase return-to-play strategies [10,11].

=== Q21
{
 "id": "Q21",
 "sourceFile": "The Role of Vitamin D in Postoperative Tendon Healing - A Scoping Review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title 'The Role of Vitamin D in Postoperative Tendon Healing: A Scoping Review' in the text matches the filename; The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine 13(10), 23259671251371300.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of 10 non-randomized studies of adults undergoing tendon repair, 8 of them on rotator cuff repair, with sample sizes from 36 to 336,320. Five rotator cuff studies linked vitamin D deficiency to higher retear or revision rates or poorer function, one found no relationship, and the biceps and lateral epicondyle studies reported associations with tendinopathy.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No randomized trials were found, MINORS scores ranged from 4 to 13 of 16 with most studies rated poor, and three studies classified deficiency by ICD codes rather than serum levels. Five studies drew on the same PearlDiver database, so patients overlap. No athletes were sampled, so applicability to athletes is inferred.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may read the association as evidence that vitamin D supplementation speeds tendon healing, when the review states causality is unproven, the studies are mostly retrospective and low quality, and nearly all data come from rotator cuff repair.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Bouchard MD, Dagher D, Keogh C, Alqahtani M, Khan M. The Role of Vitamin D in Postoperative Tendon Healing: A Scoping Review. Orthop J Sports Med. 2025;13(10):23259671251371300.",
  "doi": "10.1177/23259671251371300",
  "abstract": "This scoping review of studies on vitamin D status and tendon healing after surgery found 10 non-randomized studies, most on rotator cuff repair. Vitamin D deficiency was generally associated with delayed healing, higher retear rates and poorer functional recovery, but the evidence was low quality and largely retrospective.",
  "tldr": "Low vitamin D status is associated with poorer healing after rotator cuff repair, but the studies are weak and cannot show that correcting it helps. Vitamin D should not be used as a healing intervention on this evidence alone.",
  "methods": "Systematic search of Embase, Ovid Medline and Emcare to November 2024, following PRISMA-ScR, with two independent screeners and a third to resolve disagreements. Observational studies and RCTs of adults undergoing tendon repair were included, and quality was rated with MINORS. Results were synthesized narratively.",
  "findings": "Ten studies were included: seven retrospective cohorts, one prospective cohort, one matched case-control and one case series. Most studies (8 of 10) examined rotator cuff repair, and five of the rotator cuff studies associated vitamin D deficiency with increased risk of tears, revision surgery, retears or poorer function. Half the studies used the same PearlDiver database.",
  "limitations": "No randomized trials and no prospective data collection in most studies, with low MINORS scores. Vitamin D deficiency was defined by ICD codes in three studies, and patient overlap limits independent conclusions. No athletic populations were studied, and the authors found no research on Achilles, patellar or flexor tendons.",
  "practicalImplications": "The authors suggest clinicians consider individualized vitamin D assessment as part of perioperative care for tendon repair. The evidence does not yet support supplementation to improve healing, and prospective studies and RCTs are needed.",
  "athleteDev": "This review does not show that vitamin D improves performance. Its finding concerns tendon healing after surgery in mostly non-athlete rotator cuff patients, so it should not drive performance supplementation decisions.",
  "rtp": "Not a return-to-sport study. It cannot be used to set rehabilitation timelines or return criteria, or to recommend vitamin D supplementation as part of return-to-play planning."
 }
}

 "id": "Q22",
 "sourceFile": "The Significance of Body Surface Area to Mass Ratio for Thermal Responses to a Standardized Exercise-Heat Stress Test.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title 'The Significance of Body Surface Area to Mass Ratio for Thermal Responses to a Standardized Exercise-Heat Stress Test' in the text matches the filename; Med Sci Sports Exerc 57(1):88-93, 2025.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Retrospective analysis of heat tolerance test records for 517 Israel Defense Forces soldiers (96% men, mean age 19.8 years) tested after exertional heat illness. Heat-intolerant men had a lower body surface area to mass ratio than heat-tolerant men (248 vs 262 cm2/kg, p < 0.01), and each unit increase in the ratio was associated with an odds ratio of 0.97 for intolerance (95% CI 0.95 to 0.99); the 22 women showed a similar trend that was not statistically significant.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Retrospective registry data from one military testing program, with 96% men, so the female results are underpowered (3 heat-intolerant women). The test does not control for fitness or acclimatization, and the cohort was young soldiers rather than athletes, which the authors say may limit generalizability.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may treat a low body surface area to mass ratio as a screen for heat intolerance or as grounds to restrict return to play, when this is an observational association in one military cohort with a modest odds ratio.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Akavian I, Epstein Y, Rabotin A, Peretz S, Charkoudian N, Ketko I. The Significance of Body Surface Area to Mass Ratio for Thermal Responses to a Standardized Exercise-Heat Stress Test. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2025;57(1):88-93.",
  "doi": "10.1249/MSS.0000000000003545",
  "abstract": "A retrospective review of 517 soldiers' heat tolerance test results after exertional heat illness examined whether body surface area to mass ratio relates to heat intolerance. Heat-intolerant men had a lower ratio than heat-tolerant men, and a higher ratio was associated with lower odds of intolerance. The authors suggest the ratio may inform return-to-duty and return-to-play decisions.",
  "tldr": "In men recovering from exertional heat illness, a lower body surface area to mass ratio was linked to failing the heat tolerance test. It is one factor to weigh in return decisions, not a stand-alone screen.",
  "methods": "Retrospective reanalysis of Israel Defense Forces heat tolerance test registry data (2007 to 2021) for 517 soldiers with exertional heat illness. Heat tolerance was defined by a rectal temperature plateau in the second hour of a 2-hour treadmill test at 40 degrees C and 40% relative humidity. Groups were compared with t tests, and logistic regression adjusted for age and modelled with splines.",
  "findings": "In men, heat-intolerant soldiers had lower body surface area to mass ratio than heat-tolerant soldiers (248 vs 262 cm2/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.76). The odds ratio for intolerance was 0.97 per unit increase (95% CI 0.95 to 0.99), with the spline plateauing above about 270 cm2/kg. In women, a similar trend was not statistically significant.",
  "limitations": "Retrospective registry data from a young male military cohort, with no adjustment for fitness or acclimatization. Only 22 women were included, 3 of them heat-intolerant. Heat-intolerant men also weighed more and had higher body fat, and the authors could not rule out other causes such as reduced cardiovascular reserve.",
  "practicalImplications": "When managing return to play after exertional heat illness, a low body surface area to mass ratio may signal a higher chance of failing a heat tolerance test, most clearly in men. The authors recommend deciding return on the test result together with the athlete's history and planned activity, not on the ratio alone.",
  "athleteDev": "A low body surface area to mass ratio is one thing to note when an athlete shows poor heat tolerance on a standard test. It does not show which athletes will perform better in the heat, and the cohort was soldiers rather than athletes.",
  "rtp": "Directly relevant to return to play after exertional heat illness, but the study is observational and does not test whether the ratio predicts safe return. It should not be used alone to clear or hold an athlete, and the authors note that athletic settings with uniforms and different environments may behave differently."
 }
}

4	The Role of Vitamin D in Postoperative
5	Tendon Healing
6	A Scoping Review
7	Marc Daniel Bouchard,* MD , Danielle Dagher,y MSc , Carl Keogh,z MB, BCh, BAO (Hons),
8	LRCSI, LRCPI, Muath Alqahtani,§ MD, and Moin Khan,*||{ MD, MSc
9	Investigation performed at McMaster University, Hamilton, Canada
10	
11	Background: Tendon injuries pose significant clinical challenges because of poor vascularity and complex biomechanics, often
12	leading to suboptimal healing. While surgical advancements and rehabilitation protocols have improved outcomes, delayed heal-
13	ing and high retear rates remain prevalent. Vitamin D, a key regulator of musculoskeletal health, may influence tendon healing
14	through extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammation modulation, and cell proliferation. However, its effect on tendon repair re-
15	mains unclear, with most studies focusing on rotator cuff tendons. This scoping review synthesizes current evidence on vitamin
16	D’s role in tendon healing and identifies gaps in the literature.
17	Purpose/Hypothesis: The purpose of this scoping review is to evaluate the available literature on vitamin D’s role in tendon heal-
18	ing and its influence on postoperative recovery. It was hypothesized that vitamin D deficiency is associated with poorer healing
19	outcomes and increased failure rates.
20	Study Design: Scoping review; Level of evidence, 4.
21	Methods: A systematic search of Embase, OVID Medline, and Emcare databases was conducted through November 2024. Eli-
22	gible studies included observational studies and randomized controlled trials assessing vitamin D status in adults undergoing ten-
23	don repair. Two independent reviewers screened and extracted data, resolving discrepancies with a third reviewer. Study quality
24	was evaluated using the methodological index for non-randomized studies score. Given the heterogeneity of studies, results were
25	synthesized narratively, focusing on evidence gaps across different tendons.
26	Results: A total of 10 studies met inclusion criteria, with the majority focusing on rotator cuff repairs (n = 8). Vitamin D deficiency
27	was consistently associated with poorer postoperative outcomes, including delayed healing, higher retear rates, and
28	decreased functional recovery. Mechanistic studies suggested that vitamin D enhances healing through extracellular matrix
29	remodeling and inflammation modulation. However, the overall quality of evidence was low, with most studies being retrospec-
30	tive. Notably, half of the studies relied on the same large administrative database, leading to potential patient overlap and lim-
31	iting independent conclusions. Research on vitamin D’s role in healing other tendons, such as the Achilles, patellar, and flexor
32	tendons, was lacking.
33	Conclusion: Although evidence suggests vitamin D may support tendon healing, particularly in rotator cuff repair, studies remain
34	low quality and limited to a single tendon group. Future prospective cohort studies and randomized controlled trials are needed to
35	establish causality, assess its effects across various tendons, and determine optimal supplementation strategies.
36	Keywords: tendon healing; vitamin D; rotator cuff; tendon repair

Review


The Role of Vitamin D in Postoperative
Tendon Healing
A Scoping Review
Marc Daniel Bouchard,* MD , Danielle Dagher,y MSc , Carl Keogh,z MB, BCh, BAO (Hons),
LRCSI, LRCPI, Muath Alqahtani,§ MD, and Moin Khan,*||{ MD, MSc
Investigation performed at McMaster University, Hamilton, Canada

Background: Tendon injuries pose significant clinical challenges because of poor vascularity and complex biomechanics, often
leading to suboptimal healing. While surgical advancements and rehabilitation protocols have improved outcomes, delayed heal-
ing and high retear rates remain prevalent. Vitamin D, a key regulator of musculoskeletal health, may influence tendon healing
through extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammation modulation, and cell proliferation. However, its effect on tendon repair re-
mains unclear, with most studies focusing on rotator cuff tendons. This scoping review synthesizes current evidence on vitamin
D’s role in tendon healing and identifies gaps in the literature.
Purpose/Hypothesis: The purpose of this scoping review is to evaluate the available literature on vitamin D’s role in tendon heal-
ing and its influence on postoperative recovery. It was hypothesized that vitamin D deficiency is associated with poorer healing
outcomes and increased failure rates.
Study Design: Scoping review; Level of evidence, 4.
Methods: A systematic search of Embase, OVID Medline, and Emcare databases was conducted through November 2024. Eli-
gible studies included observational studies and randomized controlled trials assessing vitamin D status in adults undergoing ten-
don repair. Two independent reviewers screened and extracted data, resolving discrepancies with a third reviewer. Study quality
was evaluated using the methodological index for non-randomized studies score. Given the heterogeneity of studies, results were
synthesized narratively, focusing on evidence gaps across different tendons.
Results: A total of 10 studies met inclusion criteria, with the majority focusing on rotator cuff repairs (n = 8). Vitamin D deficiency
was consistently associated with poorer postoperative outcomes, including delayed healing, higher retear rates, and
decreased functional recovery. Mechanistic studies suggested that vitamin D enhances healing through extracellular matrix
remodeling and inflammation modulation. However, the overall quality of evidence was low, with most studies being retrospec-
tive. Notably, half of the studies relied on the same large administrative database, leading to potential patient overlap and lim-
iting independent conclusions. Research on vitamin D’s role in healing other tendons, such as the Achilles, patellar, and flexor
tendons, was lacking.
Conclusion: Although evidence suggests vitamin D may support tendon healing, particularly in rotator cuff repair, studies remain
low quality and limited to a single tendon group. Future prospective cohort studies and randomized controlled trials are needed to
establish causality, assess its effects across various tendons, and determine optimal supplementation strategies.
Keywords: tendon healing; vitamin D; rotator cuff; tendon repair

Purpose: To evaluate the significance of body surface area-to-mass ratio (BSA/mass) on the heat-tolerance test (HTT) results. We hypothe-
sized that individuals defined as heat tolerant (HT) would have on average higher BSA/mass compared with heat intolerant (HI) individuals.
Methods: A retrospective reanalysis of the HTT results of 517 soldiers (age, 18–38 yr; M/F, 96%:4%), who were tested by the Israel Defense
Forces HTT protocol. The criterion for heat tolerance in the current analysis was a rectal temperature (Tre) plateau during the second hour of the test. A
logistic regression analysis to evaluate the predictive power of BSA/mass for heat intolerance was performed; the spline model was applied to show the
odds for heat intolerance across BSA/mass. Results: In men BSA/mass of HI individuals was lower than HT individuals (248 ± 19 vs
262 ± 18 cm2·kg−1, P < 0.01, d = 0.76). In women a similar trend was noted but with no statistical significance between HT and HI groups. The
odd ratio for heat intolerance for every unit increase in BSA/mass was 0.97 (95% confidence interval, 0.95–0.99). The spline model plateaued above
BSA/mass of 270 cm2·kg−1. Conclusions: The results imply that body-core temperature responses to a standard exercise-heat stress (fixed external
work rate and climatic conditions) are influenced by BSA/mass. More specifically, lack of a steady state in Tre (indicating heat intolerance) was more
likely to occur with every unit decrease in BSA/mass. These findings contribute to a better understanding of the role of body anthropometry in the
response to a standard exercise-heat task that might have an implication on clinical decision making about return to duty/play of soldiers, athletes,

It highlights muscle-specific differences and gaps in adaptation research.",

The Structure, Function, and Adaptation
of Lower‑Limb Aponeuroses: Implications
for Myo‑Aponeurotic Injury
Scott Hulm1,2* , Ryan G. Timmins1,2, Jack T. Hickey2,3, Nirav Maniar1,2, Yi‑Chung Lin1,2, Katherine R. Knaus4,
Bryan C. Heiderscheit5, Silvia S. Blemker6 and David A. Opar1,2
Abstract
The aponeurosis is a large fibrous connective tissue structure within and surrounding skeletal muscle
and is a critical component of the muscle–tendon unit (MTU). Due to the lack of consensus on terminology
and the heterogeneous nature of the aponeurosis between MTUs, there are several questions that remain
unanswered. For example, the aponeurosis is often conflated with the free tendon rather than being consid-
ered an independent structure. This has subsequent implications when interpreting data regarding the struc-
ture, function, and adaptation of the aponeuroses from these studies. In recent years, a body of work
has emerged to suggest that acute injury to the myo-aponeurotic complex may have an impact on return-to-
sport timeframes and reinjury rates. Therefore, the purpose of this review is to provide a more detailed under-
standing of the morphology and mechanical behaviour common to all aponeuroses, as well as the unique
characteristics of specific lower-limb aponeuroses that are commonly injured. This review provides the prac-
titioner with a current understanding of the mechanical, material, and adaptive properties of lower limb
aponeuroses and suggests directions for future research related to the myo-aponeurotic complex.
Key points
1. In the current body of literature, there is inconsistency in the terminology and classification used to describe
and study aponeuroses. This has subsequent implications when interpreting data regarding specific aponeurotic
structures.
2. Injuries to the MTU also commonly involve damage or disruption to the aponeurosis and these injuries have
often been associated with longer return-to-play times and have higher rates of re-injury compared to isolated
muscle injuries
3. For clinicians it is important to understand the structure, function, and adaptive properties of aponeuroses as this
may provide motivation for future research to direct myo-aponeurotic injury rehabilitation and prevention strate‑
gies.

The Structure, Function, and Adaptation
of Lower‑Limb Aponeuroses: Implications
for Myo‑Aponeurotic Injury
Scott Hulm1,2* , Ryan G. Timmins1,2, Jack T. Hickey2,3, Nirav Maniar1,2, Yi‑Chung Lin1,2, Katherine R. Knaus4,
Bryan C. Heiderscheit5, Silvia S. Blemker6 and David A. Opar1,2
Abstract
The aponeurosis is a large fibrous connective tissue structure within and surrounding skeletal muscle
and is a critical component of the muscle–tendon unit (MTU). Due to the lack of consensus on terminology
and the heterogeneous nature of the aponeurosis between MTUs, there are several questions that remain
unanswered. For example, the aponeurosis is often conflated with the free tendon rather than being consid-
ered an independent structure. This has subsequent implications when interpreting data regarding the struc-
ture, function, and adaptation of the aponeuroses from these studies. In recent years, a body of work
has emerged to suggest that acute injury to the myo-aponeurotic complex may have an impact on return-to-
sport timeframes and reinjury rates. Therefore, the purpose of this review is to provide a more detailed under-
standing of the morphology and mechanical behaviour common to all aponeuroses, as well as the unique
characteristics of specific lower-limb aponeuroses that are commonly injured. This review provides the prac-
titioner with a current understanding of the mechanical, material, and adaptive properties of lower limb
aponeuroses and suggests directions for future research related to the myo-aponeurotic complex.
Key points
1. In the current body of literature, there is inconsistency in the terminology and classification used to describe
and study aponeuroses. This has subsequent implications when interpreting data regarding specific aponeurotic
structures.
2. Injuries to the MTU also commonly involve damage or disruption to the aponeurosis and these injuries have
often been associated with longer return-to-play times and have higher rates of re-injury compared to isolated
muscle injuries
3. For clinicians it is important to understand the structure, function, and adaptive properties of aponeuroses as this
may provide motivation for future research to direct myo-aponeurotic injury rehabilitation and prevention strate‑
gies.
Keywords Aponeurosis, Muscle–tendon injury, Morphology, Mechanical behaviour, Remodelling

{
 "id": "Q18",
 "sourceFile": "The Risk Factors of Hamstring Strain Injury Induced by High-Speed Running.pdf",
 "decision": "DEGRADED",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "The article's own DOI is not printed in the extracted text. Operator to verify externally; all other fields are filled.",
 "doiMissing": true,
 "identityCheck": "Title 'The Risk Factors of Hamstring Strain Injury Induced by High-Speed Running' in the text matches the filename; journal header Journal of Sports Science and Medicine (2018) 17, 650-655.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Case-control Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Track & Field"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Collegiate", "Healthy Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Prospective nested case-control study of 61 male track and field athletes (sprinters, long jumpers and decathletes) followed through one competitive season, with 18 athletes who sustained hamstring strain injuries during high-speed running matched to 18 uninjured controls. Preseason isokinetic hip and knee strength, muscle thickness, range of motion and hamstring tightness did not differ significantly between groups, and the only significant factor was a previous hamstring injury (injury ratio 25.0% in legs with a history vs 10.5% without; OR 2.85).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only 18 injury cases from one collegiate team, so power is low and the non-significant results cannot rule out associations. Injury history was obtained by questionnaire, and the tests may lack specificity to sprint running, as the authors acknowledge.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may over-read the injury-history odds ratio (OR 2.85) as a strong predictor, or read the hip range-of-motion trend (p = 0.064 and 0.095, not significant) as a real finding, when this is a small, single-team observational study.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2018,
  "citation": "Tokutake G, Kuramochi R, Murata Y, Enoki S, Koto Y, Shimizu T. The Risk Factors of Hamstring Strain Injury Induced by High-Speed Running. J Sports Sci Med. 2018;17:650-655.",
  "doi": "",
  "abstract": "Sixty-one male track and field athletes were monitored through one season, and 18 hamstring strain injuries from high-speed running were matched to 18 uninjured controls. Hip and knee strength, muscle thickness, range of motion and hamstring tightness were measured before the season, and injury history was obtained by questionnaire. Only a previous hamstring injury was significantly associated with injury.",
  "tldr": "In this small sprinter and jumper squad, a previous hamstring injury was the only factor linked to a sprint-induced hamstring strain. Preseason strength, muscle size and flexibility did not separate injured from uninjured athletes.",
  "methods": "Prospective nested case-control design in one team. Before the season, isokinetic hip and knee strength were measured at 60 deg/s, passive hip and knee range of motion and hamstring tightness by goniometer, and biceps femoris long head and gluteus maximus thickness by ultrasound. Controls were randomly sampled to match injured athletes on history and event.",
  "findings": "Eighteen athletes (29.5%) were injured during 6,258 athlete exposures, an incidence of 2.88 per 1000. Legs with a previous hamstring injury had a higher injury ratio (25.0% vs 10.5%; OR 2.85; p < 0.05). No strength, muscle thickness or tightness measure differed significantly; hip flexion and extension range of motion tended to be larger in injured athletes (p = 0.064 and 0.095).",
  "limitations": "Small sample of male collegiate athletes, all from the same team, which the authors identify as a source of selection bias. The tests may lack specificity to sprinting, and the authors note that the study cannot show these factors are unrelated to injury.",
  "practicalImplications": "Athletes with a previous hamstring strain should be treated as higher risk for a sprint-induced recurrence, so injury history belongs in monitoring. The study does not support screening sprinters on preseason isokinetic strength, muscle thickness or flexibility alone.",
  "athleteDev": "Record hamstring injury history for sprinters and jumpers, since a previous hamstring strain was the one factor associated with injury here. Preseason strength and flexibility tests did not separate injured from uninjured athletes in this sample.",
  "rtp": "Not a return-to-sport study. It does not show when an athlete can safely return after a hamstring strain and cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "populations: removed 'Injured Athletes'; athletes were uninjured at baseline and injury was the outcome ('Athletes with any pain or discomfort at recruitment were excluded')",
   "paper.limitations: attributed selection bias to the matching design -> authors attribute it to a single team ('all athletes belonged to the same team (selection bias)')",
   "paper.athleteDev: advised tracking 'sprint and jump exposure', which was not studied as a factor (event type had no significant relationship) -> record injury history only"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "Controls were matched on injury history, so the history finding comes from a leg-level comparison; the extracted Table 1 cell counts (9/27 in both columns) do not reproduce the printed 25.0% vs 10.5% ratios. A reviewer should check Table 1 in the PDF.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

 "decision": "INCLUDE",

 "evidenceSummary": "Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of 10 non-randomized studies of adults undergoing tendon repair, 8 of them on rotator cuff repair, with sample sizes from 36 to 336,320. Five rotator cuff studies linked vitamin D deficiency to a higher risk of rotator cuff tears, revision surgery, retears or poorer function, one found no relationship, the biceps study linked deficiency to tendinopathy but not to repair or revision rates, and the lateral epicondyle study suggested a possible link.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No randomized trials were found, MINORS scores ranged from 4 to 13 of 16 with most studies rated poor, and three studies classified deficiency by ICD codes rather than serum levels.  "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Bouchard MD, Dagher D, Keogh C, Alqahtani M, Khan M. The Role of Vitamin D in Postoperative Tendon Healing: A Scoping Review. Orthop J Sports Med. 2025;13(10):23259671251371300.",
  "doi": "10.1177/23259671251371300",
  "abstract": "This scoping review of studies on vitamin D status and tendon healing after surgery found 10 non-randomized studies, most on rotator cuff repair. Vitamin D deficiency was generally associated with delayed healing, higher retear rates and poorer functional recovery, but the evidence was low quality and largely retrospective.",
  "tldr": "Low vitamin D status is associated with poorer healing after rotator cuff repair, but the studies are weak and cannot show that correcting it helps. Vitamin D should not be used as a healing intervention on this evidence alone.",
  "methods": "Systematic search of Embase, Ovid Medline and Emcare to November 2024, following PRISMA-ScR, with two independent screeners and a third to resolve disagreements. Observational studies and RCTs of adults undergoing tendon repair were included, and quality was rated with MINORS. Results were synthesized narratively.",
  "findings": "Ten studies were included: seven retrospective cohorts, one prospective cohort, one matched case-control and one case series. Most studies (8 of 10) examined rotator cuff repair, and five of the rotator cuff studies associated vitamin D deficiency with increased risk of tears, revision surgery, retears or poorer function. Half the studies used the same PearlDiver database.",
  "limitations": "No randomized trials and no prospective data collection in most studies, with low MINORS scores. Vitamin D deficiency was defined by ICD codes in three studies, and patient overlap limits independent conclusions. The included cohorts were surgical patients, none described as athletes, and the authors found no research on Achilles, patellar or flexor tendons.",
  "practicalImplications": "The authors suggest clinicians consider individualized vitamin D assessment as part of perioperative care for tendon repair. The evidence does not yet support supplementation to improve healing, and prospective studies and RCTs are needed.",
  "athleteDev": "This review does not show that vitamin D improves performance. Its finding concerns tendon healing after surgery in mostly non-athlete rotator cuff patients, so it should not drive performance supplementation decisions.",
  "rtp": "Not a return-to-sport study. It cannot be used to set rehabilitation timelines or return criteria, or to recommend vitamin D supplementation as part of return-to-play planning."
 },

  ],

 }

 "id": "Q24",
 "sourceFile": "The Structure, Function, and Adaptation of Lower-Limb Aponeuroses - Implications for Myo-Aponeurotic Injury.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title 'The Structure, Function, and Adaptation of Lower-Limb Aponeuroses: Implications for Myo-Aponeurotic Injury' in the text matches the filename; Sports Medicine - Open (2024) 10:133.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified", "Professional / Elite", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Review of human lower-limb aponeurosis structure, mechanics and adaptation, drawing on PubMed studies to August 2022 found by a citation-based search. The authors report aponeurosis strain rises with contraction intensity (medial gastrocnemius anterior aponeurosis about 4 to 7% at 90 to 100% MVIC vs 1 to 4% at 10 to 30%), and that aponeurotic involvement in athletes is linked to longer return to play and higher re-injury rates; adaptation evidence rests on a few single intervention studies.",
 "screeningLimitations": "A citation-based PubMed search screened by one author, with no flow diagram or quality appraisal, so coverage may be incomplete. Many mechanical values come from small cadaver and imaging samples that are mostly not athletes, and the authors note inconsistent terminology and measurement methods across studies.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may treat aponeurosis involvement as a proven independent risk factor for hamstring or calf injury, when the authors state these properties are not yet an independent risk factor and most re-injury figures come from observational studies.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Hulm S, Timmins RG, Hickey JT, Maniar N, Lin Y-C, Knaus KR, et al. The Structure, Function, and Adaptation of Lower-Limb Aponeuroses: Implications for Myo-Aponeurotic Injury. Sports Med Open. 2024;10:133.",
  "doi": "10.1186/s40798-024-00789-3",
  "abstract": "The aponeurosis is a fibrous connective tissue within and around muscle that is often conflated with the free tendon. This review describes the structure, mechanical behaviour and adaptation of lower-limb aponeuroses, and links aponeurotic injury to longer return-to-play times and higher re-injury rates. It highlights muscle-specific differences and gaps in adaptation research.",
  "tldr": "Aponeuroses differ widely between lower-limb muscles and should not be treated as one structure or as part of the free tendon. Aponeurotic involvement in a muscle strain has been linked to longer return to play and higher re-injury, but how aponeuroses adapt to training is poorly understood.",
  "methods": "Review using a retrospective, citation-based PubMed search from inception to August 2022 on the structure, mechanics and adaptation of human lower-limb aponeuroses, with studies that did not separate the aponeurosis from the free tendon excluded. One author screened the literature, and weighted means were used to aggregate dimension and strain data where studies were homogeneous.",
  "findings": "Longitudinal strain of the medial gastrocnemius anterior aponeurosis typically ranged from 4 to 7% at 90 to 100% MVIC, compared with 1 to 4% at 10 to 30% MVIC. In athletes, aponeurotic disruption was associated with longer return to play (88 days vs 14 to 21 days in one elite Australian football study) and re-injury rates of 31 to 63% for moderate and 33 to 57% for severe aponeurotic injuries across cited studies. Two 12-week overload studies showed small increases in vastus lateralis aponeurosis width (2%) or area (7%), and one 4-week unloading study showed reduced aponeurosis stress (44.5%) and elastic modulus (29%) with increased cross-sectional area.",
  "limitations": "Single-screener, citation-based search with no quality grading. Many structural and mechanical values come from cadaver and small in vivo imaging samples, and adaptation evidence is limited to a few studies. Re-injury figures come from observational work that differs in injury classification and follow-up length, and two studies found no significant increase in re-injury within 12 months.",
  "practicalImplications": "When a hamstring or calf strain involves the aponeurosis, plan for a longer return to play, and note the injury's location and orientation (central or peripheral, transverse or longitudinal) when estimating prognosis. The authors do not yet support aponeurosis measures as independent risk factors, so the findings should inform rehabilitation planning rather than screening.",
  "athleteDev": "Aponeurosis involvement signals a more complex injury, so build longer rehabilitation into planning and check the injury type and location before progressing load. The review does not show that changing aponeurosis properties improves performance.",
  "rtp": "Directly relevant: aponeurotic injuries were associated with longer return-to-play times and higher re-injury rates in athletes, and the authors call for rehabilitation tailored to these injuries. The review cannot give a specific return-to-sport timeline, because the reported figures come from different injury classifications and observation periods."
 },
 "verification": {
